column2: ENGLISH
After Funeral

Earlier this year, your sons were still with you, and you could support them. Now they both lie buried in the church founded by the Howards, and during every Sunday mass, you see their tombstones. As your mourning continues, you realize that your husband granting you Suffolk in the event of the premature deaths of your sons makes no difference — it only shows how worthless material possessions truly are. This morning, as you rise and head toward your sons' chamber, you’re halfway there when you remember they are no longer with you. Then your maid approaches and informs you that workers, during renovation works in one of the castle’s wings, have discovered a book written by Saint Thomas More, the holy martyr beheaded by the cruel King Henry VIII — a book about lands whose knowledge was lost many years ago.
I’ll gladly read it
I’ll donate the book to the local monastery
Utopia

You open the book and read — you learn that in the 16th century, when ancestors were discovering lands now once again unknown, one of the sailors came upon an island called Utopia, whose political system reminds you of what you sometimes hear from Scandinavian merchants about the lands of the former Russian Empire. Be that as it may, as you read these revelations, a thought strikes you — perhaps you too could discover Utopia, if it ever truly existed. That thought begins to sprout within you, and it’s up to you whether you cut it down or let the tree of this idea grow.
That’s a good idea
I can’t afford to travel
Departure

When you decided to embark on the expedition, you knew there was no turning back. A day after making your decision, you informed your stewards and entrusted one of them with the management of Suffolk. You took money from the hidden deposits of your late husband and used it to fund a fleet capable of traveling great distances. Supposedly, when your former brother-in-law — Lord Howard — heard about your plans, he laughed out loud, but you no longer care. As the final preparations are completed, you set sail from Suffolk and watch the land drift farther and farther away.
I hope I won’t regret this
Lisbon

You arrive in Lisbon — here your fleet must stop to resupply. As they do, you speak with the local merchants. According to them, the route to the New Land is difficult, and they know of no one who has managed to cross it. Yet you are undeterred — you will not turn back now, not after having already set off, for that would only bring ridicule from the English nobility. After replenishing supplies and purchasing medicine for sea sickness, you set sail once again, bidding farewell to Lisbon and praying that you may see it once more.
Perhaps I will see it again
The Azores

You arrive at the Azores — this is the final stop, and the next will likely be the American mainland, where London once held possessions but lost them. The ministers of Glorian claim that the local population was incited by a demon called Washington, who promised easy riches to convince the Americans to rebel and plunder the Queen’s estates in Canada. However, since you are not a Glorian but a Catholic, you know this is all nonsense and lies. On the Azores, you hear of Brazil — a land further south of the Queen’s former holdings. A local pirate suggests that you should sail not westward, but more toward the south.
I sail west — surely Utopia lies there
I sail south
Heart of Brazil

After many days at sea, you arrive in Rio de Janeiro — the capital of the Brazilian Empire. Merchants from ships you encountered along the way told you much about this city, but now you see that their words didn’t even convey half of what you feel. The city is beautiful, the sky is clear, and you see nothing vile or ugly. It seems to you that this is what cities must have looked like before the Event. As you reach the port and disembark, several soldiers approach, salute you, and ask who you are. After you explain your mission and where you come from, their commander — somewhat surprised — informs you that the Emperor will likely want to grant you an audience within a few days. Your crew — English, Scottish, Welsh, a few Portuguese, and pirates from the Azores — is now resting, while you try to grasp at least the outline of the world the Brazilians live in.
At last, I can rest
Audience with the Emperor

As you enter, you see the Emperor upon his throne. “Behold Pedro, the Fifth of his name, of the House of Bragança, Emperor of Brazil, Protector of Guiana, etc., etc. He welcomes you into his home,” proclaims a servant, reciting the formal diplomatic formula. As a cultured person, you bow before the Emperor, and you move on to the matters at hand. The Emperor seems intrigued by you — you tell him of Britain, of the events in France and Portugal. A scribe records everything. After this lengthy conversation, which feels as if it spanned years, the Emperor appears pleased and asks that you remain longer in Brazil. He offers you a deal: you stay in Brazil for three years with your sailors, help the Emperor create a map of Europe with all its kingdoms, compile for him the basics of your language’s grammar, and write an account of the most important wars in Europe since the Event. In return, he will give you as much gold as your ships can carry.
Forgive me, Your Majesty, but I miss my siblings
Of course, Your Majesty — I will help you with your plans
Work Completed

After three long years of painstaking effort, you and your subordinates succeeded in creating everything the Emperor had asked for. Today, you handed over the series of volumes compiled with the help of your confessor and other companions, describing the wars in Europe from the time of the Event to recent years, the grammar of your language, and other matters requested by His Imperial Majesty. The Emperor is pleased, and soon you receive vast quantities of gold and provisions, with which you fill your cargo holds. Once your fleet is ready, you depart from Rio de Janeiro, knowing that you will likely never return to this city.
I will never forget this city
Farewell to Rio de Janeiro

The Emperor is not pleased with your response — clearly, he is not used to refusals. Nevertheless, he does not have you hanged or anything of the sort. Still, fearing his wrath, you do not stay in Rio de Janeiro long. After purchasing a map of the Empire, which clearly shows that Utopia no longer exists (if it ever did), you board your ship and set sail for Europe, praying that the Emperor does not change his mind and send ships after you to drag you to the bottom of the sea.
Hope dies last...
Bermuda

After many days at sea, you arrive in Bermuda — a place you imagined quite differently, once a British possession. In the port, you see a multitude of shady characters. From local merchants, you learn more — after the Event, there are two states that claim to continue the legacy of pre-Event nations: the Mexican Empire and the Holy Columbian Confederacy. The merchants tell you a lot about these countries, though their stories often contradict each other — some say the Mexicans are Christians, others claim they are pagans. Regarding the Holy Columbian Confederacy, some say it continues the legacy of the American Empire before the Event, while others, from more northern regions, claim it follows the traditions of a rebellion that once rose up against Lincoln before the Event.
We sail to the Holy Columbian Confederacy
We sail to Mexico
Veracruz

You arrive in Veracruz — a city you've never known. As you step ashore, you see a curious sight: a city battered by fate, yet still retaining some of the old splendor as part of an Empire that, according to its leaders, traces its roots back to the times before the Event. Observing the people, you notice many wear medallions — some look natural to you, while others are shocking. On one hand, you are moved by a passing procession carrying an image of the Blessed Virgin Mary
column3: on the other, you are disturbed to see some people dressed as skeletons. Soon, the city’s governor approaches you and, after questioning your origins, is surprised and asks how he can help. You tell him you came seeking Utopia — a republican state that existed before the Event — which only causes the governor’s guards to burst out laughing. The governor scolds them and says the city will take care of your fleet, and that you should travel under city guard to the capital of the Empire and speak to the Emperor ab

column2: Very well
On the road to Mexico

As you travel toward the great city, said to be a thousand years old, you pass many villages. Your confessor is disturbed by some of the practices of the Empire’s inhabitants — strange masks, talk of the holy death, and more. Halfway along the road, you encounter three riders. The soldiers escorting you want to drive them off, but you wish to speak with them. The knights, upon learning who you are, are surprised but willingly answer your questions. They say they serve the Prelate of Mexico and do not hold much loyalty to the Emperor, whom they view as idolatrous and pagan. After the conversation, you promise to pray for them and continue your journey, passing through more villages.
Okay
Mexico

You arrive in Mexico City — a beautiful place, though clearly past its golden age. One of the soldiers tells you that the Mexican Empire was once much larger, and now controls only fragments of its former lands. As you cross the gates, you see the poor staring at you with curiosity. Your confessor tells you legends of Mexican saints he heard of in seminary — of Our Lady of Guadalupe, of the Cristeros who fought against a tyrant ruler, and of many other heroes of the faith, of which only remnants remain in the capital. After passing through the slums, you reach the vicinity of the imperial palace, where you are greeted by the heir to the throne, who offers rooms for you and your entourage. You accept and ask the prince for a place where your chaplain could say Mass for you and your people. He agrees and offers an old chapel that hasn’t been used in a long time.
I feel I could be at peace here
Audience with the Emperor

After a few days of waiting, you are received by the Emperor of Mexico himself — Wenceslao III. He immediately begins asking questions about Europe, the fate of England, and other matters. He seems genuinely curious and eager to learn. Once you finish telling him about England and the current affairs, he asks you about the purpose of your journey. You tell him of Utopia — an island supposedly discovered by the Portuguese in the 16th century before the Event — and that you’re curious whether it still exists. The Emperor smiles and tells you Utopia is a fairy tale for children and that your journey was in vain. This saddens you slightly, though it doesn’t diminish the satisfaction of being somewhere no English noble has set foot for centuries. The audience lasts an hour, and as a farewell, the Emperor gives you a book written in Latin, saying it will surely interest you. You thank him, and the audience ends.
Then it's time to slowly return to Veracruz
Farewell to Mexico

You return to Veracruz — your sailors greet you with joy. It turns out that in your absence, they got into a conflict with gangs prowling the slums, which ended badly for the criminals. As a reward for weakening the city’s banditry, the governor gave them the best food in his storehouses and paid each of them the equivalent of three months’ wages in the imperial army. After thanking your sailors for their honorable conduct, your chaplain, at your request, celebrates a Mass of thanksgiving for the successful journey and the reduction of crime in Veracruz. Then, you slowly set sail from the city.
It’s time to return home
Storm

As you sail toward Charleston, the capital of the legal successor to the American Empire, a storm forces you off course. Your ship heads north and only after many days do you make landfall. You don't know where you are, as you land in the wilderness. You decide to set up camp. Once you've established order in the camp, you assign tasks: one group goes hunting, another is sent to watch for ships, and yet another is tasked with chopping firewood. You yourself await further developments.
We'll see what happens.
Patrol

After a few days, a group of riders arrives at your camp. After a brief conversation, it turns out they come from Washington and act under the authority of President Franklin Ironwrist. You decide to let them in. The delegates inform you that, by the President’s decree, docking outside of officially designated ports is currently forbidden and that you must pay a fine. To avoid trouble, you pay it, but you take the opportunity to ask the riders about the political reality of America. You learn that aside from the Holy Columbian Confederacy, there are also the Presidents who lead the Americanists and claim the title of successor to the American Empire. With this knowledge, you face a choice: either sail to a port under the President’s control or continue sailing north.
I will sail to the President’s port.
I will continue north.
Baltimore

You arrive in Baltimore – your confessor tells you that, according to some chronicles he found, this place was once a Catholic archbishopric, lasting until the Event. Regardless of whether that's true, there's no trace of the archbishopric left. People in the streets are dressed differently than in Europe. When you go ashore, you speak with merchants and learn more about the Americanists – the Presidency is not just a system of governance, but also a religious structure. What surprises you most is the role of judges – they are not only adjudicators, but also explain history to the people. After court sessions, judges speak from pulpits about American history, the threat from occultists in the north, and the metal-worshippers in the west. Since heresies do not interest you, you decide not to linger near the courts but to head quickly to Washington.
The road ahead
Washington

You arrive in Washington – from afar, you see the White House, just as you imagined it. The city is covered in banners depicting the flag of the former American Empire. As you pass through the gates, you decide to meet with someone educated – after taking advice from some local merchants, you visit a doctor. The doctor, an old man, asks where you are from, and when you tell him, he is quite surprised. You ask him to explain the situation in America. He tells you that for now, the country is divided and is a shadow of the former Empire. You are astonished when he tells you there is a man in St. Louis who claims to be the pope, and even more offended by the fact that his name is unworthy of papal dignity. When you ask about Utopia, the doctor just laughs and says you’re the first person he knows who takes it seriously. After your visit, you return to Baltimore.
Time to return
Return

Your crew hoists the sails, and you can finally feel safe. Soon, Baltimore disappears from the horizon, and you are on your way back. You see the sailors longing for home, and you know that none of them will ever forget this journey. You thank God for allowing you to live through this great adventure.
Time to return
Northbound

You sail north. Along the way, you pass New York from a distance – you recognize it by the large statue of a woman you can see in the distance. You pass many ships – some of the flags seem strangely familiar, while others are entirely foreign. The farther north you go, the colder it gets, and the boats you encounter grow more primitive. Soon, you see that the land ends – you decide to turn left and eventually enter a bay. One morning, an alarm wakes you – someone shouts: “The French! The French! They have lilies on their flags!”
This won’t be a boring day
The French

Soon, the ''French'' ship is close enough. A soldier on board signals for your fleet to stop immediately. Not wanting trouble, you give the order to comply. Shortly after, one of their ships pulls alongside yours, and a woman in armor boards your ship, accompanied by two well-armed men. She speaks French, but luckily your confessor understands and serves as an interpreter. The woman introduces herself as a member of the Ursuline Order, acting under the orders of the Mother Superior of the Ursulines in Canada. You explain your situation and say that you are from England, and your confessor is in communion with the Bishop of Rome. The woman seems surprised and pleased. She asks you to sail to Quebec so that the priest may celebrate Mass in the chapel and provide pastoral care for the local people for a while. You agree and give the order to head for Quebec.
Okay
Enemy attack

As you prepare to sail, a fleet appears on the horizon. The commander of the Ursuline fleet looks alarmed and begins issuing orders. Your confessor tells you that she is asking for your help in fighting the enemy fleet, which has recently gone to war with her order. You agree, order your sailors to arm the ship, and hide in your cabin, as it would be unseemly for a lady to fight in battle. As the battle begins, you hear the screams of the dying – suddenly a man storms into the cabin, clearly a brigand by appearance, and charges at you with a sword.
I'm too afraid to do anything
I reach for the candlestick
The attacker kills you
You manage to kill the attacker.
Aftermath

You kill the attacker – your entire outfit is drenched in blood. You stand up, and then sailors burst into the cabin. “Milady, forgive us – he got through,” they say. You nod and order them to keep fighting. You grab a sword, step out, and assess the situation. You see the Ursuline ships being set ablaze one by one. Then a sailor runs up and shouts: “Milady! That woman who commanded the French – she’s dead! The enemy commander speared her as she was surrendering!” Since your late husband once led men into battle, you know what the death of a commander means. You order a retreat eastward. After a brief clash with the enemy, you spot a breach in the enemy's encirclement and manage to escape with your fleet – though you lose three ships.
Thank God we managed to escape
Cold Lands

You reach lands where it is cold. Snow is everywhere. You thank God, you bought some furs when you leaving Suffolk. The strongest men receive them and go hunting. They soon return with seals – their meat feeds you, and their skins clothe the rest who are freezing in the hold. Soon, you encounter wanderers – one of them recognizes your language and says you're in Greenland. Now you wonder what to do: return to Quebec or go home. After a moment’s thought, you know – you’re going home.
Sail to Suffolk
Return to Suffolk

After many days, you return to Suffolk. Your lands have changed very little despite the time that has passed. As you set foot on English soil for the first time in a long while, you are greeted by your steward. He tells you that some in Parliament had already demanded you be declared dead and Suffolk handed over as inheritance but appropriate bill was blocked by a miracle. Soon afterward, you receive a letter from Lord Howard, who expresses his joy at your return. He notes that among the East Anglia burghers, the vast majority had bet you wouldn’t come back. Reportedly, only three individuals wagered their entire fortunes on your return: a half-mad bellringer from Norfolk, an old organist from the church where your sons are buried, and a Jewish fisherman from Cambridge. Now the East Anglian townsfolk will suffer serious losses, while these three—formerly nobodies in the social hierarchy—will become part of the nouveau riche elite.
There’s no place like home

You spot a raft on the horizon. As you approach, you see two soldiers aboard. It turns out that ships of the Imperial Brazilian Navy, escorting a merchant vessel nearby, had a skirmish with pirates—and lost. These shipwrecked men are officers and will now join your company.
Okay
Your ships are attacked by pirates.
We defend ourselves!

You’ve managed to win the skirmish—the pirates were routed and you captured their ships. Your sailors cheerfully transferred their supplies into your holds, and you laid your hands on the treasures left behind by the pirates.
Hurray!

Although it seemed you had the upper hand, the pirates used clever tactics. They launched fire ships at your fleet and initiated a boarding attack. Some of your sailors had to extinguish fires on the upper decks while the rest were being slaughtered by the pirates. You rush out of your cabin, and before you can grasp what’s happening, you’re struck by three arrows, tumble down the stairs, and bleed out as you catch a glimpse of your crew fighting for their lives.
I will die...?
Blood of Jane Neots

This character is a descendant of Jane Neots — an English lady of Suffolk who, after losing her two sons, organized a successful expedition to America, effectively rediscovering it for England and earning her place in history as the only known female geographical explorer.
Royal Administration

The Royal Administration System is based on old laws and acts of the British Crown, which make this system similar to feudalism despite differences with the elevated role of Parliament, tendencies towards isolationism from European affairs and the improved station of trade companies.

FitzSpatstone Blood

This figure is a descendant of Edwin FitzSpatstone, Poet of Albion and first Lord Regent of the Kingdom of Britain. This leader is famous for overthrowing the Windsors and codifying the beliefs of the Glorians.
Dismantle Northern Authonomy

The autonomy of Northern England under the Prince of York was a compromise reached during the reign of Lord Protector Aleister FitzSpatstone in 2526. After a series of wars in Northern England, an agreement was reached that granted Northern England, with its capital in York, broad autonomy under the nominal authority of the Lord Protector. This autonomy was sanctioned by the Compromise Act of 2527, which once again confirmed the North's broad autonomy. Today, when relations with the North are well established and the local elites are on our side, perhaps it is time to abolish this autonomy.
End of Yorkist Authonomy

The autonomy of Northern England under the Prince of York was a compromise reached during the reign of Lord Protector Aleister FitzSpatstone in 2526. After a series of wars in Northern England, an agreement was reached that granted Northern England, with its capital in York, broad autonomy under the nominal authority of the Lord Protector. This autonomy was sanctioned by the Compromise Act of 2527, which once again confirmed the North's extensive autonomy. Today, with relations with the North well-established and the local elites on our side, this autonomy has been abolished, and the Compromise Act of 1527 has become history – the territories of Northern England are now under the direct jurisdiction of the Lord Protector and the British Crown.
Now, we can say goodbye to this old act
Go on a pilgrimage

While pilgrimages are not as popular among the Virgin Queen's followers as they are among Christians, there are those who faithfully make pilgrimages to places associated with the Imperial Crown and its legacy. You, too, could be one of them.
I shall go to pilgrimage to seek Queen's grace in one of the holy places of british history.
I will start making travel plans.
Pilgrimage

There are a number of diffrent holy places that you could visit on your pilgrimage. All of them are considered most sacred in our Queen's eyes, but a somewhat closed destination might mean a safer journey.
I will visit London

You reach London, the ancient capital of the Virgin Queen's great empire. In the distance, you see Westminster Abbey—where the greatest ceremonies in all of Albion once took place. But you continue on, passing streets filled with merchants, travelers, and the people of London themselves. And on you go, you see the former Houses of Parliament in the distance—today it's a ruin, but perhaps one day the Virgin Queen will return and rebuild it herself, casting it once more in gold, silver, and platinum, to make it a more magnificent house than ever, capable of housing all of Parliament and all those whom the Queen most delights. Soon, you reach the ruins of Parliament—people like you are already gathering there, eager to pay their respects to the Pearl of Albion.

You reach Oxford, A monument to English culture and learning, the place where, many years ago, when London was threatened, Parliament met and enacted laws binding all of Albion. It was here that, over the years, great names and minds were forged to the glory of the Queen. You reach this city and see in the distance the old university—a forge of elites. You walk there, fight your way through crowds of locals, other pilgrims, and students, then reach the university and descend into the old university chapel to pay homage to the one to whom you made the pilgrimage.

You arrive in Glastonbury, an old town near Somerset. This unassuming place for a foreigner is very important to the locals. You visit Glastonbury Priory, or rather its ruins. Among these ruins, you see countless candles lit by pilgrims and locals. Outsiders claim that one of England's kings destroyed this monastery centuries ago, but no devout follower of the Virgin Queen would ever believe it. Legends say that prayers were held here before the Event in honor of the Virgin Queen, and that the Knights of the Round Table swore allegiance to King Arthur, who was to be buried within the Abbey grounds. After visiting the old priory, you ascend to Glastonbury Tor, from where you can observe the entire town at a glance, just as the heroes of the Round Table did centuries ago.

You arrive in Perth, an ancient Scottish city. The city looks beautiful from afar, but for a devout worshipper of the Virgin Queen, something else is important—something permanent, not fleeting like beauty. You pass the inhabitants of Perth and walk a long way until you reach Scone Palace, the coronation site of Scotland's kings. You pass other visitors who also wanted to visit this ancient complex—soon you reach the place where the Scots moved the stone—and so you stand before one of the corridors and see it, the sacred stone of Scone on which every Scottish king was crowned.

You reach Calais, city that for many years was a legacy of British genius and power, and one of the jewels of the British imperial crown. Although there are few traces of the Virgin Queen's former power left. In the distance, you see fishermen setting sail—who knows, perhaps they'll find debris from the crushed galleons of the demonic Great Armada, whose commanders were wizards and warriors of evil, who using their spells and illusionistic tricks, sought to kill the Virgin Queen and make Albion a living hell. But you don't wait for them to find anything—you head further, to the ruins of an ancient castle where the Queen's steward resided for many years, standing on the fringes of her vast empire, guarding the land of milk and water against the barbarians from the south and east, there to pay homage to him and your Queen.

You arrive in Leicester, city little known but rich in history. More famous is the field near the city, Bosworth Field, where many years ago, in the fateful year of 1485, Richmond defeated the usurper Richard III, a tyrant and murderer of his innocent nephews. On the way to Leicester, you pass this field and pay homage to those who fought for the Red Rose, before entering Leicester. You see the city's ancient buildings, and as you pass Leicester Cathedral, you see a statue of a man holding a sword in one hand and raising a crown in the other. Some say this statue represents King Robert Hood, others Henry VII. One thing is certain, this city fills you with an aura that no other city has ever possessed.

You arrive at Tilbury. It was here, over 1,000 years ago, that Queen Gloriana gathered with her army to defend Albion from the demonic Great Armada and delivered her unforgettable speech, which instilled courage in the hearts of all gathered, so that not one of them faltered or faltered during the battle with the Spanish. You see this village and you don't see the glory, but you know it's there. Here, on this beaten earth, stood many thousands of brave Englishmen, ready to shed their blood for Albion.

You reach Stratford-upon-Avon, where, hundreds of years ago, the greatest bard of all time was born: William Shakespeare, who immortalized the wickedness of Richard III and Macbeth and portrayed the virtues of Henry VII and the Virgin Queen. You pass through the streets of this ancient city, seeing old buildings that recall the memorable times before the Event. You're glad you've come to this small but important town. You enter the old Holy Trinity Church, where, according to legend, Shakespeare's grave lies, and after a moment, you spot him. The statue of the Bard of Avon hasn't survived well, but the inscription has. You read it and it reads: "Stay, passenger, why goest thou by so fast? Read, if thou canst, whom envious death hath placed, Within this monument: Shakespeare, with whom, Quick nature died
column3: whose name doth deck this tomb, Far more than cost, sith all that he hath writ, Leaves living art but page to serve his wit".

Long live the Virgin Queen!
Parsifal and Lohengrin, come with me here!
Kings of Beloved Scottish Land, I am with you!

Long live the Virgin Queen!

You finally return home after this pilgrimage. You feel it has taught you some lessons, including a lesson in homesickness.
Everywhere is nice, but in home is nicest...

In addition to the more famous places of pilgrimage such as London, Oxford, Calais, Glastonbury and Perth, there are others less frequented such as Leicester and nearby Bosworth, Tilbury and Stratford-upon-Avon, the hometown of Master Shakespeare.
I shall visit Bosworth and Leicester
I shall visit Tilbury

As a worshipper of the Virgin Queen, you can choose from other places important to her: the ancient Glastonbury Abbey where King Arthur was buried, Calais, a stronghold of the Crown, or Perth, the most important place for ancient Scottish kings.
I shall visit Glastonbury
I shall visit Perth

As you walk along a rather old, ancient road, you see two roadmen walking towards you.

During your journey, you reach a provincial town. You hear from several people that a cricket tournament is taking place there, a team sport that has long been a common practice in Albion, strengthening bonds between people regardless of social class. The people you meet urge you to attend the match and perhaps even bet on one of the teams.
Go to the match
Go further
Cricket match

You walk towards the pitch where a cricket match is about to take place. You enter the stands, where a heated debate is taking place. Some claim that the home team will win, having practiced all night and all day for this important match. Others claim that the guests team will win, having also caught up with the economy in terms of time devoted to practice. From a distance, you hear a man calling for bets on one team or the other.
Bet on the home team
Bet on the away team
I bet on noone
Even though the team you bet on has a good chance of winning, they ultimately lose. You lose your bet and leave the stands with a loss.
Money gone down the drain
Despite the high risk that the team you bet on will lose, you ultimately win. You win your bet and emerge from the stands with a profit.
Easy win
You sit and watch the cricket match the entire match. When the home team wins, you leave rejoicing in their victory.
Nice match

Along the way, you pass a troupe of musicians who have stopped nearby. They sing a long and captivating ballad about how Henry V set out for France with his soldiers and, on St. Crispin's Day, fought a battle against the French rebels for the glory of Albion and the Crown, which he won by drowning the greatest wicked men of France in blood. Remembrance Day is a special day. On this day, everyone forgets the present and focuses on the past, on the times when Britain, in alliance with France, fought against the German Empire in France, where thousands of the flower of the old empire marched to their deaths. Following an old custom, everyone you see in the city carries natural or artificial poppies sewn onto their clothing, paying tribute to the soldiers of yore. An hour before noon, there is a two-minute silence, during which everyone remains silent. Then, a mourning ceremony takes place, and you and the others gather in the central square. A trumpeter from a nearby temple tower plays the Last Post on his trumpet, then a closer orchestra plays traditional melodies, and the choir joins in singing. The official ceremony, full of speeches and songs, concludes with the playing of the Ode of Remembrance. After this ceremony, people disperse to enjoy this special day in other ways.
